speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Chairman, I beg to move "That the total sum to be allocated for Head T of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These challenges have generally been met with much appreciation as mitigating solutions against the backdrop of escalating rents and housing prices.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am in full support of Minister Desmond Lee's commitment in ensuring better access and affordable public housing for Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Affordable housing is often a debated topic in cities across the world.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It impacts people's lives and their long-term family or career planning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For Singapore, it entails a continuous effort to balance the multitude of conflicting needs from ensuring affordable housing with a growing population and limited land availability, exercising inclusivity for different segments in society and evolving our public housing to meet the future aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I wish to ask the Minister to provide a holistic picture of how MND intends to address the housing demand in the next five years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Further, I hope to hear how more effort will be placed to support the following three group of people for their housing needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, interim housing for divorcees with special needs children.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: A divorce and its aftermath are always challenging to deal with, much less for individuals who have to single-handedly care for special needs children in the process of the divorce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The challenges exacerbate when they have no certainty of a place to live in when the matrimonial flat is going to be sold.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Without a final Court judgment, they are also unable to rent interim housing from HDB and most have difficulty renting from the open market since the landlords are unwilling to rent any rooms, given their child's condition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Under the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS), married couples and family units who have booked an uncompleted unit are able to obtain interim rental from HDB.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In Budget 2024, more concessions and expansion have been made to these couples and families via the PPHS Open Market Voucher.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While these initiatives align with Singapore's pro-family stance, in which I am also supportive, we cannot overlook and deny the evolving and changing family structure that is happening.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The second group, seniors who have no family support.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population in Singapore, much has been discussed on how best to age in place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Many initiatives have been introduced, ranging from the Lease Buyback Scheme (LBS) to the introduction of 3G flats, Married Child Priority Scheme to encourage intergenerational living and even subsidies to enable an elder-friendly home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Indeed, it is heart-warming to see how HDB has evolved in designing housing spaces based on multigenerational assumptions to allow more solitary seniors to mingle.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While the hardware and infrastructure are essential for ageing in place, the psychological and emotional aspects of our seniors cannot be neglected.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The third group, families with a foreigner spouse.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With Singaporeans being more globalised, there is an increasing trend of cross-national marriages.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I have received many anecdotal sharings during the Meet-the-People sessions and interactions with my residents where some revealed that having a foreigner spouse makes them feel disadvantaged living in Singapore, the reason being as they relocate back from overseas work or they married a foreign spouse with plans to set up their family in Singapore, they encounter difficulties in securing affordable home options with their spouse as a family unit.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Family planning is always critical for many of them and access to public housing is an important first step as they enter a different phase in their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While I totally understand the rationale of the current rules are meant to protect our public housing supply, which is already heavily subsidised, there is an increasing group of Singaporeans who need homes to raise the next generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: After all, it is the roof over our heads that give us peace of mind to focus on work and to raise families and also other aspects of life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While I acknowledge MND has certainly put in tremendous efforts to ensure Singaporeans have access to affordable homes, the work will continue and it needs to continue to evolve as we deal with the changing family unit structures and the future aspiring lifestyles of our population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also affected contractors who are involved in other major HDB works, such as electricity load upgrading projects, car park upgrading projects, amongst others, all of which are multi-year projects.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my constituency of Eunos in Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC), one particular car park upgrading project has been ongoing for a considerable period of time, with the expected completion date of the project extended two times already.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Contract extensions also come with an increase in costs that were not considered originally for HDB projects that are undertaken by Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Re-tendering a partly-completed project at current prices means that costs will have to be incurred.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would HDB consider helping contractors and Town Councils with additional support to complete these projects, the disruptions of which could not have been anticipated at the time of tender, if necessary?

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: Mr Henry Kwek, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Mr Chairperson, I would first like to talk about housing affordability for young couples.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In particular, I would like to talk about one specific group.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These are the young couples from low-income households who are looking to settle down soon.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I think that across the board, the schemes' affordability for most young couples is good.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is this particular group that I am more concerned about, which is, the young couples from low-income households looking to settle down soon.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even if they are both working, it could take time or years for this group to save up for the downpayment for the BTO, especially if they applied for the BTO during their student days.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Is there more that MND and HDB can do to ease the cash flow burden of this particular group of young Singaporeans so that they can be financially secure to start their family?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And how much additional subsidies will HDB have to allocate for the Plus and Prime housing in the coming years?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I understand that HDB can only provide a range of estimates of additional budget, but those estimates will be helpful.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP's Millennial Apartments Scheme is a strategy to make up for the inherent long waiting time under the BTO scheme and to address the current acute shortage of alternative housing options for married couples, young families or groups of singles.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The long waiting time for BTO flats is widely regarded to have a significant negative effect on our Total Fertility Rate (TFR).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Millennial apartments are smaller in size, so HDB can build more flats on the same plot of land to ease the current housing pressure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The smaller quality rental flats are rented out on a two- to five-year basis for Singaporeans who are waiting for their BTO flats or singles who want to live independently.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will provide medium-term housing stability for young Singaporeans while they figure out their life plans and longer-term housing needs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Millennial Apartments Scheme is also a strategy to rejuvenate our Central Business District (CBD) and mature estates by creating a vibrant young community in each of them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In place of the Prime and Plus Housing schemes, Progress Singapore Party recommends that affordable, high-quality interim rental apartments to be built at these locations to offer a broad range of young Singaporeans a chance to live in a prime area at least once in their lifetime.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By concentrating young people together, we can even improve their prospects on dating apps that work by location.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By having our young people living, working and socialising in these locations, our CBD and surrounding areas can become more vibrant like Shibuya and Shinjuku in Tokyo or Tsim Sha Tsui in Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The older mature estates, such as Marine Parade, Bedok and Ang Mo Kio, need rejuvenation too.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These estates were developed rapidly within a short period of time and their 99-year leases will consequently come to an end at about the same time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The demographic profile of these estates is also becoming older.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can start redeveloping these estates now, by redeveloping some older blocks of flats into Millennial Apartments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope that the Millennial Apartments Scheme will be a game-changer that will relief the pressure on couples to rush to secure a flat and give young Singaporeans more choice to fulfil their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge all young Singaporeans to consider and decide for yourself whether Progress Singapore Party's Millennial Apartments Scheme is superior to what the People's Action Party Government has to offer today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And HDB does not have to do this by itself.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There is, today, a vibrant market with commercial players so HDB can partner private operators, but set standards, including in pricing and affordability; and take the lead in developing the market.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This will further enhance housing options for our singles to meet their diverse needs and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, having a roof over one's head is a necessity in a person's life.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as the Forward Singapore exercise ostensibly shows that the condominium is no longer part of the Singapore dream, having a place to stay, even on a rented basis, provides a sense of stability, security and shelter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Over a year ago, I asked the Minister whether the Government would consider providing further market subsidies for qualifying applicants for schemes, like the PPHS and the Public Rental Scheme (PRS), in order to support young parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have also suggested that we cannot rely on the open market to be a catch-all solution for the people who are unable to avail themselves of such rental schemes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the time, the response from the Minister was that providing subsidies or grants for renting flats in the open market is likely to induce demand and drive up market rents, which will compound rather than help solve problems.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are the first steps on a broader path to meeting varied housing needs, something which I have raised in an adjournment Motion in Parliament in 2021.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would also like to thank the Minister for increasing his tolerance of potential distortionary effects from subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure the couples that stand to benefit from the subsidies are likewise appreciative.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Although the growth in rent has moderated, we cannot rest on our laurels.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The need for more widespread rental options to support the wider population beyond specific targeted group remains.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From demographic groups like S Pass holders who need a place to stay to individuals who need to move out on their own for varied reasons, the demand in the market for affordable housing, even if on a temporary basis, remains.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even other Ministries are not blind to this problem.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In August last year, the Ministry of Health (MOH) sought operators for a planned series of hostels for the foreign healthcare workforce, recognising that they needed support in finding affordable accommodation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to ensure that rental accommodation options are expanded to prevent the crowding out of local demand for HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, there is great comfort in having a nice home to rest and recharge in – physically, emotionally and mentally.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For some people, a restful home may be an elusive concept if there is frequent conflict, arguments or violence in their families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Another group is young singles below 35 that I meet often in my Meet-the-People sessions, who are unable to have a restful home because of chronic toxicity or conflicts in their familial relationships.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The third group are single parents, who struggle to find resources for care in order to hold down jobs.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Local research has shown that the causes of inequality and poverty in Singapore is more complicated than we assume.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: More Singaporeans now recognise and have empathy for the physical and mental hazards of public rental living.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: An informal poll I conducted on my Facebook page, revealed overwhelming support for more to be done for public rental housing.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can provide better options – co-living options for singles, communal living formats and better-designed public rental flats, so that restful, pleasant and supportive homes can be made available to everyone.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As I have shared in my earlier adjournment Motion on this topic, experience in other countries have shown that living environments have the power to increase self-esteem and confidence which in turn motivates individuals, contributing to positive rehabilitative outcomes.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Commune-based living formats can foster effective mutual support and resource-sharing for those, who otherwise struggle by themselves, such as single parent families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For young people, living apart from their families of origin can also help to individuate themselves successfully and healthily.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Individuation is the development of a clearer sense of self, separate from our parents and others around them.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is critical in our maturing process and one's mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Housing, therefore, can help us achieve social mobility and well-being outcomes, far beyond just serving the physical function of a shelter.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: That way, people of diverse backgrounds and circumstances can rent affordably when they need to, as a transition phase.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This can bring benefits, such as better social integration and the pulling of diverse social capital that enhances social mobility.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Our public housing projects, such as Pinnacle@Duxton, have won international awards.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I dream and I hope that our public rental housing, such as the one just down the road from it at Jalan Kukoh, will one day be no longer known as the slum of Singapore but as a rehabilitative and incubation space for those who eventually emerge from their difficult circumstances, like phoenixes from adversity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, I have encountered more residents seeking help to appeal for a PRS JSS unit but have faced difficulties finding a suitable co-applicant even after receiving a list of potential co-applicants from HDB.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Other than the JSS-OR scheme, what other measures are HDB exploring to assist this segment?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: What is the occupancy rate and what are the eligibility criteria for a family wishing to apply for a 3-room PRS unit?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have met many of whom, are anxious about housing for themselves and their children following a divorce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: While waiting for their matrimonial flat to be disposed of, they are unable to apply for a PRS unit.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But if they apply only after the matrimonial unit is sold, they may be in for a long wait before the application for a PRS is approved and a unit is allocated to them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: During the wait, they have no stable housing.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In many cases, the financial proceeds from the sales of matrimonial units are insufficient for them to secure a new flat and they also cannot afford renting from the open market.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I would to ask, what is the Government's outlook on public housing demand in the next five years?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I ask, with the cognisance that forecasting demand is far from a precise science and many people have got it wrong before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To date, the Government has approached the issue of urban renewal of public housing in two ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS), identifies projects for urban renewal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But economic viability of SERS is limited by whether a more intensive redevelopment of a given site is even possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, this then led to the Government's Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is less clarity about how much compensation exactly this would entail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The main attraction of VERS then, is that it will offer leaseholders at least a vote to remain in their homes; although doing so, could inadvertently, impede more systematic urban renewal efforts as well as long-term town planning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, while SERS offers non-trivial compensation to affected leaseholders, it has also attracted some controversy especially when residents prefer the status quo of remaining in their homes instead of forced relocation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, VERS is voluntary, but the Government runs into the difficulty of securing buy-in from residents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While there is no indication to date as to the voting threshold required for selection, it is by definition more than 0%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2019, the Workers' Party released a working paper on alternatives to address the issue of lease decay and affordable housing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our paper offered policy proposals, including a universal sale and lease buyback scheme, a more widespread SERS programme and an expanded public rental scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our expanded SERS proposal will, however, be bound by similar challenges of ensuring economic viability and securing buy-in as the Government's own programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If more intensified redevelopment does not yield sufficient economies of scale in and of itself, the taxpayer will have to absorb part of the costs in the name of the public benefits of urban renewal and ensuring that the population, indeed, has a roof over their heads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One potential middle-ground approach between the largely voluntary nature of VERS and the compulsory stipulation of SERS, is to introduce moving voting thresholds for passage of a VERS project.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These thresholds would shift as the lease winds down, making an upvote easier when renewal needs become ever more pressing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, a flat with 50 years' lease remaining may require a 75% supermajority; but one with half the time remaining, could perhaps, only need a simple 50%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This allows homeowners to both have a say on whether they choose to move but at the same time, respect the need for systematic urban renewal.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, in an expensive open rental market, the PPHS is often families' only practical option for finding a home ahead of their own, ahead of BTO completion.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of my PAP colleagues and I have called for more rental housing diversity and support.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am grateful for MND's shifts in this regard.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is heartening that HDB has temporarily set aside the catered flats in Tanglin Halt for interim housing, allowing the number of PPHS flats to increase.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What demand-side factors have led to these announcements and why the period of one year, given some BTO flats may take a longer time to complete?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can expectant parents qualify for both schemes and what is the Government's target average waiting time for families to obtain a flat under this scheme?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government explore any kind of priority scheme?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the BTO scheme was introduced in 2001 after the Asian Financial Crisis in 1997 resulted in HDB being left with a large stock of unsold flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One major downside of the BTO scheme is longer waiting times of four years or more.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Young Singaporeans are marrying later and many of them want to have their own homes before marrying or having children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that the longer waiting time will have an adverse effect on our TFR.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although resale flats and private properties are options for couples to get their homes faster, their prices are much higher and beyond the reach of many.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is less than half of the replacement rate of 2.1 and has serious economic and social consequences.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can we adjust our housing policies to arrest the falling TFR and support parenthood?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP had proposed the Millennial Apartments Scheme to provide interim rental housing to young people to address this problem.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Mr Leong Mun Wai, has spoken on this in greater detail earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP would also like to propose two other policy changes for consideration which can help young Singaporeans start their families earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, increase the number of flats with Shorter Waiting Times where flats are built in advance in a departure from the BTO approach to half of the projected annual demand based on marriage and immigration numbers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, lower the age limit for singles to buy HDB flats to 28 and allow them to buy new 3-room flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This way, when they find the right partner, they can start their family immediately if they already own a flat.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Low TFR has troubled us for very long.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is strange that single unwed parents do not qualify for the PPHS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Single parents who are divorced or widowed qualify for PPHS, so why not single unwed parents?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A single unwed parent recently approached me for help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She intends to apply for a BTO flat but like so many Singaporeans, she needs a place to stay while the flat is being built.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is especially difficult for her to rent a room in the open market as many do not want to rent to those with young children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Renting from the open market for more than three years will deplete her savings significantly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know we do allow single unwed parents to obtain PPHS but on a case-by-case basis, but this adds stress to someone who is already stressed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my Parliamentary Question (PQ) filed in October 2022, I suggested, given the tight supply of PPHS flats, that these couples be provided with grants to enable them to rent flats from the market directly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because I met several couples who were balloted out and they were also unable to afford to pay rent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: MND, in its response, stated that such action will, and I quote, “likely induce demand and may drive up market rentals which would be counterproductive as it makes renting more expensive”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the Government’s decision, may I ask what steps are being taken to minimise the concern that MND expressed in response to my PQ?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the wait for BTOs is usually more than one year, how is it proposed that we deal with the “cliff” effect after the expiry of one year?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I speak again on the issue of lift upgrading for the six blocks of HDB flats in Hougang SMC, where there are still certain flats which do not have same-floor lift access, as I have done every year since 2021.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am glad that HDB has finally agreed to provide LUP to these residents of mine, though I am still none the wiser of why there was a change of mind.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I continue to speak for the remaining five HDB blocks in Hougang.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is a very real issue affecting a number of my residents, especially those with mobility needs requiring assistance to assess the stairs outside their units when they have to go out, not to mention inconveniences or risks when ambulances are dispatched.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have said previously that I would feel the pain when residents told me that their parents or grandparents had to be carried when accessing the stairs next to their unit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Residents also have to pay additional charges for delivery items.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Lift Access Housing Grant is not an option for many residents with whom I have spoken to on this issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is never easy to ask people to shift to a different address and it is definitely not an empathetic solution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many residents still cannot accept HDB's explanation of the issue of cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask the Government to explain to affected residents of each affected block the true reasons for LUP not being available to that block.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is it due to cost, and if so, how much it would cost and how much would residents have to pay?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For residents whose blocks have technical constraints, let the residents know.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Please also inform residents of the alternative mechanical options available and the costs involved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And please inform the Town Councils so that they can convey the same explanation when asked.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, I would also like to convey some feedback arising from the recent LUP polling exercise at Block 833.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One, there are residents in the same block who, while not eligible to vote, may be affected by the LUP construction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, their flat may be partially blocked by the new lift shaft, or they have other concerns such as privacy or other disamenity issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Two, HDB should have an information centre handling enquiries regarding the LUP at the HDB Hougang office instead of requiring residents to go to one at Serangoon North, since the Hougang office is just a short walk away.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Three, the LUP handbook should be given to residents in the same block much earlier than just one week before the main polling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also hope that HDB can arrange for a copy of such handbooks to be delivered to the Town Council office at the time of delivery to residents, so that the Town Council and I can refer to it when we attend to residents' feedback on the LUP.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will be at the Old Airport, Jalan Dua and Jalan Batu area.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some residents complain that they had carried out repairs to the spalling concrete on several occasions, but the defects recur again and again.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are also occasions when the slabs of concrete peel off from the ceiling and fall onto the ground.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: You can even see the steel reinforce bars on the ceiling.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I had previously invited HDB to consider some of these flats for SERS, but unfortunately, it was turned down.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In this case, may I volunteer to MND for my block of flats to be prioritised for this HIP too?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Then, the residents can then have some assurance that the living environment of their flats will continue to be safe and secure, and that their estate will remain vibrant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, the Lift Replacement Fund was introduced during the 2017 amendment to the Town Council's Act.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It addresses the substantial deferred costs associated with lift renewals in our ageing estates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This provision ensures minimum disruption due to lift breakdowns for our residents, notably the elderly, young children and those with mobility challenges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, the current apportionment of service and conservancy charges and Government grants, which is 26% to the Sinking Fund, 14% to the Lift Replacement Fund (LRF), may be precipitating a skewed emphasis towards the LRF.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Looking at the 17 Town Council's latest annual reports, I noticed that for many of them, their LRF is expanding at a significantly faster pace compared to their Sinking Fund.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The stipulated use of the LRF may be unduly restrictive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These recommendations seek a more efficient balance between addressing current exigencies and future preparations, assuring all residents benefit from dependable lift and escalator facilities.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Chairman, Mdm Er, a resident of Nanyang, recently approached me with a pressing issue regarding her living situation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, their circumstances have changed significantly since then.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Their seven-year-old son has been diagnosed with myopathy, causing muscle weakness and rendering him unable to walk independently.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As he grows heavier, Mdm Er struggles to carry him up and down the stairs to reach the HDB lift.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many occupants of these flats purchased their homes when they were young and did not anticipate mobility issues.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, as they age, navigating the stairs to reach the lift becomes increasingly challenging.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Er has attempted to apply for the Lift Access Housing Grant, she has encountered numerous hurdles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In addition, it is understood that MND has been hesitant to install lifts at these blocks due to technical challenges, although advancements in technology could potentially address these constraints.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Even if residents are required to contribute more financially to cover the costs of these additional lifts as compared to other usual Lift Upgrading Programmes, many of them will still likely to support as they treasure their mobility and accessibility needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This poses significant challenges for various upgrading projects, such as the Neighbourhood Renewal Programme (NRP), Estate Upgrading Programme (EUP) and Revitalisation of Shops (ROS) Programme, including those in Nanyang.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: These rising costs have led to budget constraints and the need to sacrifice essential features in the approved projects.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, in one of my EUP, I have to sacrifice building even the playground as well as these sports facilities for those who exercise.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In light of these challenges, I would like to inquire with MND regarding the frequency of budget reviews for these upgrading programmes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is crucial to ensure that these upgrading programmes continue to effectively enhance the quality of living in our neighbourhoods, despite the financial challenges posed by rising construction costs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Therefore, proactive measures to review and potentially adjust budgets are essential to ensure the successful implementation of these projects and the well-being of residents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This could potentially contain the race to the bottom or race to the top, depending on one's point of view, behaviour of coffee shop operators; and, in turn, short circuit the pass-through of high tender prices to high rents; and, in turn, high rents to high food prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am pleased to see that in Sengkang, a new NEA-run hawker centre has opened up in Sengkang Grand Mall in Buangkok and another is slated to open at The Village in Anchorville.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I believe that increased competition among vendors will, at the margin, likewise help control the rapid rate of food price increases seen islandwide since the start of the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But both of these cannot be the full story.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, if the Government truly believes that competition alone would be sufficient, it would not have ceased selling coffee shops to private operators since 1998.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In contrast, there is no such assurance for private operators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And in our conversations with stall vendors, many have shared that back-breaking rent increases have forced them to either pass-through costs to their meal prices or risk giving up their tenancy altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If we are unconvinced that rental increases may be well-contained by competition alone, it may make sense to return control of our coffee shop to HDB hands with the outright purchasing of existing units if necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In addition to being able to exercise greater control over rental price hikes, which it has already demonstrated a willingness to do, this will undoubtedly help Singaporeans who are struggling with expensive meal prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One alternative is to incrementally increase the weight placed on the quality of the bid for every additional budget meal the tenderer includes in its bid, or to receive a percentage discount on their final bid price that increases as the number of budget meals offered increases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These options are featured in HDB's BudgetMealGoWhere website.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have received positive feedback on this and would like to convey my appreciation to HDB.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the older HDB estates, however, the budget meals and drinks options are still limited.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is because most of the coffee shops there are sold in the open market and not rented from HDB.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Minister mentioned that HDB is studying the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To address current food affordability concerns, I suggest that the study be completed sooner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I also seek an update on the status of the matter.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The objective was to reimagine Singapore's future together, shaped by Singaporeans aspirations and visions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I personally participated in some of these engagements.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It was gratifying to witness the premium that many Singaporeans placed on sustainability and the consistent emphasis of ensuring Singapore is liveable for the future generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Saying Singapore has land scarcity is an understatement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Question is, how can we better utilise, transform and reallocate land parcels, visualise and plan future towns to fulfill the changing needs?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: There is no doubt that land use or exchange for different designated purpose of land parcels receive much scrutiny by the public today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It is even harder when we have to take into consideration the need to preserve our biodiversity or heritage at specific locations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The traditional way of viewing existing land allocation is through the demarcation of the Core Central Region (CCR), Outside Central Region (OCR) and Rest of Central Region (RCR).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: However, with the growing acceptance of work-from-home and evolving lifestyle needs, there is no longer a need where prime activities are conducted only in central region.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: People also wish for shorter commutes between where they work, live and play.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This can be seen in the drive for Jurong's transformation and Punggol Digital District.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: So, what will future industrial areas be like?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Can we support more economic activities and build industry verticals that are stacked in the same building or clustered in the same zones?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: All these require long-term planning and support from the market-led forces.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The infrastructures will also not be complete without the greenery, recreational and transportation nodes that provide connectivity between towns.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: With Singapore being one of the most densely-populated countries in the world, the decision to conserve native green spaces, regrowth of secondary forests and other forms of vegetated sites will have an impact on our environment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Such planning requires expertise from different domains and even tapping on global experts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Less has been said about the WetBulb Global Temperature (WBGT).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Both the urban heat island (UHI) effect and WBGT, are important indicators of heat-related stress on the human body at work or at play in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Researching the UHI and the WBGT brings about questions on ensuring liveability and a high quality of life for Singaporeans in the long-term.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: There are many factors that contribute to liveability but today, I would like to talk about population density as it is a factor that can intensify the UHI.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: While this may not be near the population density of certain cities, however, given that Singapore is a country and not just a city, once we break it down further to measure the density of actual liveable space, such as by excluding roads, offshore islands or even industrial estates, the reality can be quite different.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: How do URA and HDB measure the population density of our towns and estates?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: For example, if and when HDB measures population density of a HDB town, does it use the total land area or the residential area?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Taking this distinction from HDB's publication entitled "Key Statistics – HDB Annual Report 2021-2022".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Next, how do URA and HDB take into account population density for the building of our towns, estates and residential homes?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: URA and HDB should assess the population density of our HDB towns and private estates and consider whether we need to make any adjustment to the density of any of our towns or estates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Measuring density by estate is important because when you have high densities in certain regions over others, what the everyday Singaporean experience is the rush of the crowd where they live when they go about their day-to-day activity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This is further exacerbated by MND's decentralisation strategy, which is to reduce congestion in Singapore by bringing jobs closer to homes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Higher population density is also a key contributor to a higher urban temperature.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: And while some of the urban temperature caused by UHI can be mitigated through infrastructure planning, the day-to-day rush observed by Singaporeans in denser locales is harder to control.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Does HDB evaluate and compare the population density of all HDB towns to ensure that each town's population density is at a comparable healthy level; and mitigation measures should, perhaps, be carried out to reduce the density in some of the towns with higher density?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: For residents of the denser towns and areas, what is being done to reduce the UHI and the WBGT?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Can we ensure that upstream planning norms also take into consideration the population density of estates rather than looking at greenfield or brownfield sites available for public and private housing launches?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Ultimately, my question to the Government is this: how do we ensure that Singapore remains liveable for the everyday Singaporean, beyond those that have privilege to live in less-dense areas or estates like Bukit Timah or Sentosa?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Delivery freelancers who I speak with in my capacity with NTUC's National Delivery Champions Association (NDCA), share their pride in delivering on time barring terrible weather or traffic.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In turn, how might we ensure that our living spaces are safe work environments for delivery persons?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, gated residences, such as condominiums, often require visitors to register to enter.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They might also have designated visitor parking spaces.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Those of us who played hosts during the recent Lunar New Year, would surely have desired for your guests to receive a courteous experience at the security post and a safe and easy-to-navigate passage across the compound to your home.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We would not have wanted our guests to bear with the indignities of having to surrender excessive personal data to the security, traverse slippery and uneven surfaces, or locate specific units without visible signages or reliable mobile reception.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We would also not have wanted our guests to risk their lives and property because they were disallowed from entering the compound and had to alight at the road.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Worryingly, these are recurring concerns shared by our delivery freelancers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They share that the feedback is often acknowledged by stakeholders, but seldom acted on.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We are hopeful that the Workgroup will be a longer-term platform to engender delivery-friendly infrastructure and workflow improvements.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, safer, gracious and timely deliveries take more than just hardware.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to put forth three questions to the Minister.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, it is inevitable that disputes might arise between delivery persons and condominium representatives.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Graciousness thrives in an ecosystem where care and consideration are mainstays.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: How might the Ministry foster care and consideration between condominium representatives, residents and external providers, such as delivery freelancers?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, in 2021, the Ministry invited Singaporeans to join in the Long-Term Plan Review to share their views on their vision for Singapore's development for the next 50 years and beyond.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry share the criteria for incorporating their suggestions and ideas for Singapore's land use plans?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will MND take into account the feedback from the public while drafting DMP 2025?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can MND provide an update on the main developments that we can look forward to?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is DMP 2025 different from previous master plans?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given Singapore's limited land, with increasingly more competing uses and development priorities, such as for the expanding agri-food sector, housing, commercial buildings, light and heavy industries, greenery and parks, intensification of land use is the only way forward.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to build up so that we can free up the land for our farms, reservoirs, parks and retain our nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The convenience of being able to complete multiple tasks at the same location will allow residents to save on time as well as cost for commuting.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Planning more mixed-use zones within our residential communities will allow us to achieve these objectives.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During a previous debate for Committee of Supply MND, I had advocated for "whole-of-precinct" and "whole-of-estate" redevelopment concepts for older estates.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This approach would improve the land parcellation and road network for more optimal accessibility and connectivity.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Intensification of land use is also achieved, where there is an integration of various public and commercial amenities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Take, for example, Tampines Hub, which hosts multiple Government agencies and a range of amenities, from medical to social, such as community health centre; family medicine clinic; sports facilities, including a gym and swimming pools; library; hawker centre; retail shops; and a community club.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Development of a town has been done mostly in a linear manner in the past.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the Bishan estate where I serve has many standalone amenities housed in mainly single-purpose buildings.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Junction 8 shopping mall, which opened in 1994, is situated between the Bishan MRT interchange and the 35-year-old bus interchange.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Within the vicinity are two old buildings: the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Bishan, completed in 1997; and Bishan National Library, completed in 2006.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A few condominiums were completed in Bishan in recent years.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With more households moving into Bishan, the redevelopment of the central Bishan area into an amenities hub would be highly desirable.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the Bishan estate moves into its fifth decade, it is an opportune time to regenerate Bishan Town Centre with an enlarged modern shopping mall that will incorporate the uniquely Singapore feature of wet market and hawker centre.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Medical, social and sports facilities, such as swimming complex, CPF Building, library and a polyclinic, could be further integrated with a bimodal transport interchanges of the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) and bus.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such integration would enhance connectivity and accessibility, especially for the ageing cohorts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Green plots in the vicinity could be included as part of the land intensification and integration project.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From an environmental perspective, this considered approach can potentially reduce new construction requirements whilst the reduced commute for residents can also lower the carbon footprint from the use of transport.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given that the holistic planning of a precinct will likely have impact on existing buildings, the Government can consider the selective application of Selective Enbloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) and Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS) where relevant.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: VERS is presently reserved for select precincts that are 70 years or older.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the objectives of the redevelopment are intensification of land use and bringing more convenience to residents rather than rejuvenation, is it possible to have more flexibility in terms of the eligibility criteria for the age of the estate?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Other criteria, such as current density of the estate versus the ideal intensity and accessibility and availability of amenities, should be considered more relevant.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Prime Minister Lee had announced VERS in his 2018 National Day Rally speech.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In his speech, Prime Minister Lee had mentioned that VERS would allow HDB to redevelop older estates in an orderly way, paced over 20 to 30 years, instead of four or five years at the end of the leases of many old HDB towns.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Prime Minister Lee noted that the Government needs to work out the selection of the precincts, the timing of the redevelopments, compensations and how to afford the Scheme.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has been six years since the announcement.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I urge MND to consider clearer and more direct financial assistance for persons with disabilities (PwDs) to cover improvement works in their HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This needs to be clearly indicated on the EASE webpage for improved visibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: MND must take steps to design housing policies that are inclusive and accommodate PwDs, enabling them to live independently and participate fully in society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ensure that PwDs have access to housing options that are conveniently located near essential amenities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Access to things like MRT stations, healthcare facilities and community services is vital for PwDs to minimise daily friction.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, could MND prioritise PwDs for flats near these amenities?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Enhanced Proximity Housing Grant (PHG) would lessen the financial burden that comes with purchasing a home near family members, particularly when they might already be living in a comparatively pricier area.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Chairperson, Age Well SG is an important initiative that many PAP Senior Group Members of Parliament (MPs), including myself, have been championing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: What are the likely features and expected cost to our citizens?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: With regard to upgrading the public spaces of matured estates, will HDB partner with Town Council to do improvement works or at least provide a budget for Town Council to implement?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: What are the key features that will be enhanced and what is the anticipated timeline?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: And if Town Council is involved, can HDB communicate the parameters to Town Councils soon so that Town Council can deconflict upcoming upgrading plans?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: This is because some of the Town Councils, including mine, have already started building many senior-friendly infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Therefore, if the funding can be used to build other types of senior-friendly features, such as upgrading the surrounding areas of Active Ageing Centres (AACs) and senior gathering points, which are outside the declared areas covered under Age Well SG, that will be much appreciated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, as a rapidly ageing society in Singapore, the Government has made concerted efforts over the years to ensure that we can sustainably and compassionately address our seniors' needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A growing number of seniors are expressing their desire to live out their golden years in familiar neighbourhoods or in spaces where they retain as much independence as their health conditions allow.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, efforts to make society more senior and caregiver-friendly start from revamping and reimagining our neighbourhoods and homes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not just a matter of barrier-free access or painting murals on blocks, but how can we also co-locate services closer to our seniors and caregivers?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we build common amenities so that more neighbours can spot warning signs early and we can all be eyes and ears on the ground for seniors who are struggling with dementia, mental health, aggravated health conditions or even caregiver burnout?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Outside of homes, can public spaces be better curated to encourage intergenerational support within the community?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry also provide an update on seniors' reception to things, such as community care apartments in Bedok?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there plans to expand the community care apartments to new locations in the future?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Ministry also provide details on the implementation, scope and eligibility of towns for Age Well SG?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given that several neighbourhoods are old and it would be costly to revamp our estates, what specific upgrades are envisioned to common spaces beyond aesthetic enhancements and how will these lead to an enhancement of our seniors' daily lives?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is an issue if they are unable to get time off during working hours or if someone falls sick at night, especially if they are families with young children or elderly residents themselves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As a result, health conditions sometimes go untreated.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Moreover, under Healthier SG, these general practitioner (GP) clinics will also offer a wide range of services – from routine check-ups to vaccinations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, ensuring that GPs are available at convenient locations and at extended hours is not just a matter of convenience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is a matter of equity, accessibility and public health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some may say that this would be too expensive to give out incentives for clinics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But, in reality, this is not an island-wide issue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In many town centres, there is no shortage of such clinics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Rather than a broad policy, the Government could look at localised needs and apply the levers in a targeted way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The same analysis could be done for other essential services and amenities, such as hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As the overall population gets more affluent, having lower-cost options on hand becomes particularly important to ensure no one is left behind.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What is the Government doing to ensure the provision of such essential services in our neighbourhood commercial centres?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, while the existing tender system for commercial units within HDB estates offers some variety through different categories like supermarkets, eating houses and other shops, it lacks centralised planning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: This would be followed by ensuring a balanced mix of retail categories, including F&B, grocery stores and shops for daily necessities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: HDB should consider residents’ demographics and conduct outreach activities to ensure offerings are relevant and accessible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: A vibrant mix of shops and amenities not only enhances convenience but also fosters a sense of community and belonging.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Onerous tendering requirements, inconvenient invoicing processes, lengthy payment delays and bundled contracts create financial strain for many SMEs in today's high-cost capital environment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can we leverage technology to digitalise the end-to-end payment process and expedite settlements?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Government also implement regular milestone payments on a quarterly basis, aligned with project progress, rather than paying a lump-sum only upon project completion?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Bundled contracts also raise concerns about limited flexibility and risk absorption, especially during unforeseen circumstances like the recent pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Ministry explore alternative approaches to mitigate these risks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How will it empower local contractors and SMEs, to participate meaningfully in the construction sector?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The Government has done a lot for the construction industry during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: However, the industry is facing a fair amount of challenges, with several major main contractors going bankrupt and an ongoing credit crunch in the overall industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: What more can the Government do to support contractors to tide through the current challenging industry conditions right now?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I believe there are a number of instances where agencies will approve large VOs at the tail end of the project period, due to the complexity of the project, which creates cash flow problems for contractors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As such, a prompt whole-of-Government review of VO process to allow for partial payment of large-ticket VOs would benefit the construction industry at this juncture.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Building and Construction Authority (BCA) has set the Price Quality Method (PQM) for the evaluation of public sector tenders.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These are construction tenders under the BCA Construction Workheads, which are estimated at $3 million and above.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This framework assigns a range of weightages and scores price and non-price attributes to evaluate the construction tenders.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The tenderer with the highest combined PQM score would be selected for award.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would give them a higher chance to take part in the larger construction projects and this would also support the development of capabilities by our local construction companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope to see more local construction companies to win large infrastructural projects in Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The Industry Transformation Map (ITM) is often keenly watched by industry players for it signals the strategic focus of the Government for the respective industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In recent years, modular construction has been gaining popularity with results demonstrating its promise of improving completion rates over traditional construction methods.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Further, this industry remains highly challenged by labour shortage with little signs of improvement in this respect ahead.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Indeed, digitalisation has its promise of helping to enhance efficiency with companies such as BHCC Construction and Pan-United Corporation being beneficiaries of these technologies resulting in cost and manpower savings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Some also demonstrated on their production processes and workflow that embracing artificial intelligence and virtual reality enabled more productivity and workers improving their work skills while adopting digital technologies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Despite advancement in technological developments, industry players have revealed that the Built Environment sector is still very traditional and has been a laggard in adopting technologies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Reasons for such are aplenty, ranging from adopting new technologies hindered by a mindset of “why fix it when nothing is broken” to outright resistance due to unfamiliarity of such technologies or concerns over long lead-time and high cost in embarking on digitalisation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Should the progress be slow, will more efforts be put in by the Government to encourage technology adoption?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Singapore has set a target to achieve net zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The bulk of buildings we have today is the existing stock of older buildings which may be less energy-efficient.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Can MND provide further updates on how we are helping owners of such buildings to transit?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A recent report revealed that Singapore has lost 37% of our biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What we have left is precious and we must protect and treasure it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I understand the need for development, the need to provide housing for fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The middle ground must be a strong Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Law to minimise the impact of our development.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This, however, is not just about embedding the EIAs in our planning permissions or issuing guidelines for developers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is about enshrining the EIA in a specific piece of legislation, standalone, and ensuring that we enforce this strong piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have pushed for this for many years now and I am not sure what is holding us back from ensuring that we protect our remaining green spaces in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is time to have a proper, strong and robust EIA Law in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In our Adjournment Motion last year, together with Ms Nadia Samdin, we spoke about the rich biodiversity in the waters around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We shared about our passionate youth marine advocates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our marine ecosystem deserve protection and they are also our protection against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need all the help we can get in our fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has been 10 years since we designated Sisters’ Islands as a marine park and it has benefited greatly from the protection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is time to consider expanding this protection to other key areas, such as the waters around Pulau Ubin, Pulau Jong and Lazarus Island, to name a few.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Chairman, as our country continues to urbanise and develop, it is more important than ever for Singaporeans to have access to opportunities to connect easily with nature.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Whether it is through admiring greenery while exercising on our park connectors or being able to live in harmony with native wildlife, who are equally part of our country too, appreciating a city in nature means understanding the trade-offs and both the upsides and inconveniences.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: What efforts has the National Parks Board (NParks) made to involve more members of the community in transforming Singapore, including developing an understanding and appreciation for nature and its impact on our lives?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: A thriving city in nature necessarily entails more flora and fauna, including an increase in human-wildlife interactions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: It shows that our native biodiversity is growing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: However, there have been calls asking for intervention to curb wildlife populations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: What more can the Government do to manage human-urban wildlife tensions?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Further, threats of animal-related diseases have increased in recent years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: What key bio-surveillance efforts is the Ministry currently undertaking?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: A thoughtful approach to preserving Singapore's blue spaces is essential.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: This offers not only new opportunities for Singaporeans to connect with our oceans, but also contribute to national goals such as coastal protection and flood resilience.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: And how does the Government expect this development to affect marine life in the Singapore Straits?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Has the Government assessed any impact on nature and wildlife on and around the islands?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: And what other pilot ecotourism concepts are being considered for the southern islands?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: As Chairman of a Town Council, I spend quite a bit of time dealing with complaints about pigeon feeders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Residents complain about the feeding of pigeons and how the pigeon faeces makes a mess of their clothes, windows; how pigeons would fly or walk into the food centre and attack the food while residents are having their meals.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: We spend an inordinate amount of time dealing with the mess caused by pigeons due to the actions of a few inconsiderate pigeon feeders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The law on feeding of pigeons is clear.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: It is illegal, and pigeon faeces are a health hazard.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: All these issues could be mitigated if we have greater enforcement against pigeon feeders, and this was also reflected in a Straits Times article on 11 December last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Some of the residents who could tell me exactly which of their neighbour is throwing rice or bread onto the grass patch and to feed the pigeons regularly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: But yet, when we pass the information to NParks, the usual answer is that they are unable to get evidence of the pigeon feeder.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Fine them, jail them or even send them for mental health treatment if they are found to have compulsive behaviour and cannot stop feeding pigeons.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Let us make the living environment better for all our residents instead of being held hostage by a few irresponsible pigeon feeders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Science tells us that reducing food sources is the best way to bring down the bird population.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I know that gathering evidence of bird feeding is not easy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We can do more to help our enforcement officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will the Ministry consider introducing a similar statutory presumption for the offence of wildlife feeding under the Wildlife Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This will help our enforcement officers significantly, reduce the amount of bird feeding and address public concerns on this issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is not merely a statistic, it is a depressing reality that speaks volumes about our society’s graciousness and regard for life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is a call to review our animal welfare and protection laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: First, we need to address the inadequacy of penalties for acts of animal abuse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In comparison, vandalism carries a penalty of $2,000 fine, imprisonment of up to three years and caning of between three to eight strokes for certain first-time offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will the Government consider increasing the jail term for animal abuse so that we protect our animals as strongly as we protect our property?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As promised by Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How last year, we are not pussyfooting around the issue of keeping cats in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As much as the agencies are tired of me asking repeated questions on this, I am also tired of asking this every year for the past few years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But this change in policy must make sense.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: One of the reasons we banned the keeping of cats in HDB is because of caterwauling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have experienced this firsthand when I used to live in Jurong West and I agree these cats make loud mating calls in the middle of the night.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, we are now proposing to allow the keeping of cats in HDB but not mandate the sterilisation of pet cats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We are setting ourselves up for future problems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In reversing the ban, we need to make sure we resolve the reasons for the ban in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mandating sterilisation also ensures people do not end up with too many cats as the cats will start breeding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I hope the Government will hear the calls from animal welfare groups and ensure we mandate the sterilisation of pet cats as a prerequisite for the keeping of cats in HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Singapore, we have a large population of seniors and as an ageing population, this phenomenon will only increase.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is important for us to prevent loneliness as well as isolation, because all these, if allowed to continue, can lead to a serious deterioration for our seniors physically and mentally.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, it is important that in our living built environment, we design this with our seniors in mind so that as much as possible, they are able to live independently and gracefully.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even amongst our seniors, there are those who are more vulnerable but there are also those who are fitter.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Regardless, as we all age, there will come a time where we need to be able to care for ourselves, even with caregivers, and to be able to move around independently, and lead meaningful life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Ministry, how are they going to design new estates as well as old mature estates such that socialisation is enabled?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And two, for new estates, it is easy to design from scratch, but for the more mature estates where a lot of things are already built up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, how are we going to refine, repair and enhance them so that they are safe for use and at the same time, encourage social gatherings of our seniors – from the void decks to the covered walkways to pavements and so on?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can we also pick up pace in enhancing these areas?
